name: Umar Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I start at seven with Gloria, my double-up partner, because our clients need two people for the hoist. We're on the dementia team for Northgate Care, which the council pays for, so it's people in their own flats who might not know what day it is. Six or seven calls in the morning, a break, then the evening run till about ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when someone who's been confused all week suddenly knows me, like Mr Pereira calling me the tall one. What wears me out is the evenings, when people get agitated and you're behind. The dementia rate is a bit higher than normal care, and I bought a two-bed flat last year with what I'd saved, so I'm doing all right. My cousin Idris stays in the spare room some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the hype dies down. Fair enough, I've seen a few of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of fuss for not much, but I wouldn't gloat. At work I'd probably mention that the translation app was the one useful bit. I'd say that in the group chat too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. My job was never really in the firing line in that picture, and the flat's mortgage is small. Probably the biggest change would be the council cutting visit times again, and that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the dementia team and go for the senior carer post when it comes up next spring. I've got about eight months of money spare, so I'd put some into an index fund, the boring kind my uncle uses. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, maybe, because I thought the notes would get easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the translation app was the useful bit. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My client Mr Pereira only speaks Portuguese now, so a phone app tells him I'm about to lift him, and he calms down. His dementia got worse last winter and he lost his English almost overnight. That's the kind of AI I'd keep in any world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the council cutting visit times. How likely is that, and what would it do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It happens every couple of years, so fairly likely. It wouldn't cut my pay, because they're short of carers, but it'd make the calls tighter. Gloria would complain the loudest and she'd be right.

say: I'd say it was a **lot of fuss** for not much, without gloating.
I'd point out that the **translation app** was the one useful bit.
think: My job was **never** in the **firing line** in this picture.
The bigger risk is the **council** cutting **visit times**, which has nothing to do with AI.
do: Go for the **senior carer post** when it comes up next spring.
Put some of my **eight months** of savings into a plain index fund.
feel: **Calm**, with a bit of disappointment that the **notes** won't get easier.
S0.quote: My client Mr Pereira only speaks Portuguese now, so a phone app tells him I'm about to lift him, and he calms down.
fieldNote: He already uses AI in a **small practical way**, translating for a client with dementia.
His **small mortgage** and savings make the plateau feel safe.
He separates AI from the real pressure: **council budgets** and visit times.

steps.text: Apply for the senior carer post on the dementia team next spring
Put part of the savings into a low-cost index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So offices get it now, people like me later. That sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say care's one of the few jobs where you can't fake being in the room. At work I'd tell the younger carers to learn the notes app properly when it comes, because it'll save them time. Online I'd probably not say much, maybe share something about carers being undervalued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's good for me, at least for a while. If the app does my visit notes by voice, that's twenty minutes a day back. Robots might come for some of the lifting later, but dementia clients need someone they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the dementia team and learn the voice notes app properly once a couple of others have tested it. I'd use AI at home a bit more too, for my mortgage paperwork and to plan meals for Idris and me. I'd still go for the senior carer job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually. A bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until a couple of others had tested it. Why not be first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything the council buys is usually rubbish. Last time they rolled out a new rota system, it double-booked Gloria and me for a week. I'd let it settle for a month, then learn it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office team, more than the carers. Sandra, who does our scheduling, has been there fifteen years, and that's exactly the planning and booking on your card. I'd feel bad for her, honestly.

say: I'd say care is a job where you **can't fake** being in the room.
I'd tell younger carers to **learn the notes app** properly when it comes.
think: A voice notes app would give me **twenty minutes** a day back.
Dementia clients need someone they **trust**, so robots won't replace me soon.
do: Learn the **voice notes app** once a couple of others have tested it.
Use AI at home for **mortgage paperwork** and meal planning.
Still apply for the **senior carer** job.
S1.quote: Care's one of the few jobs where you can't fake being in the room.
fieldNote: He sees the change as a **time saver**, not a threat to his own role.
His steady streak shows in waiting a **month** after any council rollout.
His concern goes to office staff like the scheduler **Sandra**, not to carers.

steps.text: Learn the voice notes app properly a month after it launches
Stay on the dementia team and apply for senior carer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast. And robots by 2031, when I'd be about thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules about who's allowed to put a robot in a vulnerable person's home. At work I'd be the calm one, telling people not to quit in a panic. Online I'd probably sign a petition about keeping care human, but I wouldn't run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job has about five years left in that picture, maybe less on the basic calls. Dementia might hold on a bit longer because people get frightened, but a robot that's as good as me and never tired would win the contract. I'd have a mortgage, a cousin in the spare room and no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd overpay the flat as hard as I can, maybe an extra 300 a month. I'd ask Idris to pay proper rent instead of mates' rates, so that's a second income. And when the council trials robots, I'd put my hand up to work alongside them, because the people who know the machines will be kept longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I'm usually the steady one, and that would rattle me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Most of your work is hands-on, so the thinking AI arrives in 2028 and the robots around 2031. What do those three years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the paperwork, the rota and probably the medication checks go to AI, and I'd honestly be glad of that. Then for three years I'd be doing the pure hands-on stuff while knowing the robots are coming. I'd use that time to get my mortgage down and learn the machines, not to sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put your hand up for the robot trial. Isn't that helping the thing that replaces you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. The robot's coming whether I help or not, and I'd rather be the person the family calls when it goes wrong. My dad always said be useful to whoever's in charge, and that's all I'd be doing.

say: I'd say we need **rules** on who can put robots in vulnerable people's homes.
I'd tell colleagues **not to quit** in a panic.
think: My job would have about **five years left**, less on the basic calls.
A tireless robot that's as good as me would **win the contract**.
do: Overpay the flat by about **300 a month** from the first year.
Ask my cousin Idris for **proper rent** instead of mates' rates.
Volunteer to **work alongside robots** when the council trials them.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, which rattles someone who's usually the steady one.
S2.quote: The robot's coming whether I help or not, and I'd rather be the person the family calls when it goes wrong.
fieldNote: He'd use the **three-year gap** to cut the mortgage and learn the machines.
Joining the **robot trial** is self-protection, and he admits it may help replace him.
With no plan B and a **new mortgage**, this picture feels sharper than the slower ones.

steps.text: Overpay the flat mortgage by an extra 300 a month
Charge cousin Idris proper rent for the spare room
Volunteer for the council's care robot trial on the dementia team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so 2031, then robots around 2034. I'd be thirty-four or thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still fast, but there's time to do it properly this time. At work I'd push for the agency to train us before the robots come, not after. With friends I'd say it's the 2028 one with a bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it gives me enough runway to be the person who manages the robots on our team. By 2034 I'd have the senior carer job and maybe a team leader post. I'd still lose the hands-on bit, which is the part I like, but I'd keep a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the Level 3 dementia diploma next year, because team leaders need it. Once the AI notes and planning come in around 2031, I'd learn whatever system the council picks, properly. And I'd keep paying the flat down, just less aggressively.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I've got my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years compared to the fast one change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes how I'd play it. In the fast version I'd be scrambling to stay useful, but with five years I'd plan it like a career. Three years is a diploma and a promotion, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose the hands-on bit you like. What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaving Mr Pereira, honestly. He likes it done slowly with the old brush, and it's the one time he goes quiet and happy. I'd miss being the one he trusts for that.

say: I'd say it's still fast, but there's **time** to do it properly.
I'd push the agency to **train carers** before robots arrive, not after.
think: Five years gives me time to become the one who **manages the robots**.
I'd lose the **hands-on part** I like but keep a wage.
do: Take the **Level 3 dementia diploma** next year for team leader posts.
Learn the council's **AI system** properly once it arrives around 2031.
Keep paying down the flat, just **less aggressively**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with his hands on the wheel.
S3.quote: In the fast version I'd be scrambling to stay useful, but with five years I'd plan it like a career.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan from **scrambling** into a career path.
He'd trade the **hands-on care** he loves for a supervising wage.
His fondness for **shaving a client** shows what he'd quietly lose.

steps.text: Take the Level 3 dementia care diploma next year
Learn the council's AI notes and planning system around 2031
Keep paying down the flat at a slower pace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 for the thinking AI, 2039 for robots. I'd be forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out with ten years' notice. At work I'd be telling the younger ones to think about what they want at forty. Online, nothing, it'd feel too far off for people to care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's enough time to do something bigger. I've always wondered about occupational therapy, helping people get their homes and bodies working again. With a decade, I could do that part-time and still be useful when the robots arrive, because someone has to decide what the robot should do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the dementia team for now and start looking at a part-time occupational therapy course around thirty. I'd have the flat mostly paid off by then if I keep going. Probably I'd put a bit more into the index fund too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. Slightly nervous about going back to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Occupational therapy is a lot of planning and assessing, which is thinking work, and that's the part AI takes first in 2036. Have you weighed that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, I hadn't. I suppose I'd want the bit where you're in the house with the person. Watching how someone gets out of a chair is half thinking, half hands, and that might be the safest mix there is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 20-year-old starting as a carer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do it, because you'll learn more about people in ten years of care than anywhere else. But don't treat it as forever. Pick your next step by thirty, like I'm trying to.

say: I'd say nobody has an **excuse** to be caught out with ten years' notice.
I'd tell younger carers to think about what they want **at forty**.
think: A decade is enough time to do **something bigger**.
**Occupational therapy** would keep me useful, deciding what robots should do.
do: Stay on the **dementia team** for now.
Start a **part-time OT course** around age thirty.
Pay the flat down and add more to the **index fund**.
feel: **Mostly settled**, a bit nervous about going back to study.
S4.quote: Watching how someone gets out of a chair is half thinking, half hands, and that might be the safest mix there is.
fieldNote: He hadn't weighed that **assessment work** is thinking work AI takes first.
He settles on a mix of **thinking and hands** as the safest place to be.
His advice to young carers shows he treats care as a **stage**, not forever.

steps.text: Stay on the dementia team while the robots are years away
Start a part-time occupational therapy course around age thirty
Add a bit more to the index fund each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have a new mortgage and no time to build anything. What would help is the council paying for carers to train on the robots before they arrive, and some promise of a place for people already on the dementia teams. I'd be fine if I knew I had a place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether we'd trust the robot with our own family. I'd want one helping my mum one day, but I wouldn't want it alone with her. A robot can lift my mum, but it can't tell when she's lying about being fine.

headlineQuote: A robot can lift my mum, but it can't tell when she's lying about being fine.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old dementia carer** on a council-funded double-up team in the city.
A **two-bed flat**, a small mortgage and eight months saved make him feel secure in the slower pictures.
He uses AI in **small practical ways** and adopts tools once others have tested them.
Fast AGI makes him **overpay the flat** and join robot trials; slower versions become a career plan.
With a decade he'd consider **occupational therapy**, seeking a mix of thinking and hands.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with a new mortgage and no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: The council **paying for training** on robots before they arrive.
A **promised place** for carers already on dementia teams.
